Present Appeal has been preferred u/s.29 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act,
2005 (hereinafter referred as PWDV Act) challenging the order dated 14.02.2024 whereby the trial court has directed Mohit Arora (hereinafter VIRENDER KUMAR referred as respondent) to pay Rs.5000/- per month to the BANSAL complainant Smt. Bindiya Kandhari (hereinafter referred as complainant/appellant) towards maintenance of the daughter by VIRENDER from the date of filing of the petition till she attains the majority 15:10:41 +0530 and has not awarded any maintenance so far as the complainant/appellant is concerned.
2.

sentences.text: The brief facts giving rise to the present appeal are that the complainant/appellant got married with the respondent on 04.05.2001 as per Hindu rites and customs.
Out of the wedlock, one female child namely Kalindi Arora was born on 21.03.2002.
It is alleged that the appellant and the respondent are living separately since 07.10.2014.
The appellant has filed the petition under the provisions of PWDV Act.
An application for interim maintenance was also moved, which was allowed and the court passed the order of maintenance as mentioned above.

Aggrieved by the order,

sentences.text: 3. Notice of appeal was sent to the respondent.
Trial court record was also requisitioned.
4. I have heard the Ld. Counsel for the complainant/ appellant, Ld. Counsel for the respondent and perused the record.
5. Ld.
Counsel for the complainant/appellant submitted that the trial court has not exercised its judicial discretion judiciously resulting into miscarriage and failure of justice.

Ld. Trial Court has wrongly assessed the interim maintenance considering the minimum wages @ Rs.14842/- per month whereas minimum wages in India, as per the educational qualification of respondent, is Rs.23,082/- per month, in accordance with the notification of the Labour Commissioner dated 23.10.2023.

Ld. Trial Court has also failed to appreciate that the respondent is B.Com. Pass, doing business under the name & style of Kalindi, earning sufficiently and much better in comparison with the complainant, who is home maker and bearing the responsibility of maintaining and upbringing the daughter solely taking financial aid from the parents since separation.

The mother has to not only take care of the child and spend money on her upbringing but also has to spend substantial time and make efforts and, therefore, the quantum of maintenance should have been decided accordingly.
6. The daughter of the complainant/appellant is still pursuing her studies and is unable to maintain herself.
The child has to be taken care till she is able to maintain herself and not on attaining the majority.
The trial court has not considered this fact and restricted the right of maintenance till attaining the majority.
Obligation of the respondent herein is to maintain his unmarried daughter till she is able to maintain herself out of her own earnings till she gets the employment.
Even the complainant/ appellant has now lost the job in August 2021 regarding which she has already filed the document but the Ld. Trial Court has not considered this fact.
She has made lots of efforts but she is not getting any job but the trial court has failed to appreciate this fact and also that respondent is living a lavish life.
He has concealed his financial status though the trial court has mentioned this fact but still has not awarded the maintenance as required.

7. The daughter of the complainant/appellant has specific and essential financial needs,
encompassing education, healthcare and basic necessities and it is the duty and responsibility of the respondent to fulfill the same.
The trial court has totally failed to consider and appreciate the material facts.

It is prayed that the maintenance awarded be enhanced and instead of restricting it to the date of attaining of majority, it be till she gets married and the appellant be also awarded maintenance from August 2021 since when she is not employed.
8.

sentences.text: During the course of arguments, learned counsel for the petitioner/husband was asked if any document has been filed to support his contention that the respondent/wife was practising and earning.
However, he was unable to show any document in support.

A perusal of the record would show that besides placing on record the aforesaid bio data of the respondent/wife, which is disputed, the petition/husband has not placed any document on record to show that the respondent/wife is actually earning.

8. In Shalija and Anr. v. Khobbana reported as 2017(2) RCR (Criminal) 497 : (2018)
12 SCC 199, it was held that 'capable of earning' and 'actual earning' are two different requirements.

The Family Court has recorded in the impugned order that any amount paid as maintenance in favor of the respondent/wife and her minor child for the period in question would be liable to be adjusted.
10. In view of the above discussions, I find no illegality or perversity in the impugned order passed by the Family Court.

Though it was sought to be submitted by the learned counsel for the respondent,
and by the respondent himself that he has no source of income as his party business has now been closed, the Court is neither impressed by nor is ready to accept such submissions.
The respondent being an able-bodied, he is obliged to earn by legitimate means and maintain his wife and the minor child.

Having regard to the evidence of the appellant-wife before the Family Court, and having regard to the other evidence on record, the Court has no hesitation in holding that though the respondent had sufficient source of income and was able- bodied, had failed and neglected to maintain the appellants.

Considering the totality of facts and circumstances, we deem it proper to grant maintenance allowance of Rs.10,000/- per month to the appellant-wife, over and above the maintenance allowance of Rs.
6,000/- granted by the Family Court to the appellant no. 2-son."

sentences.text: " 4. Only submission of the learned counsel for the appellant to challenge the order impugned is that the appellant herein is unemployed and he has no source of income.

This bald assertion made by the appellant in the objection filed in the proceeding under section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act has been disbelieved by the family court.
5.
The second submission is that the respondent wife has independent income as she is running a medical store along with his father who is a doctor.

6. Dealing with this submission of the learned counsel for the appellant, suffice it to note that mere fact that the respondent wife is educated and is doing something to survive since she has been thrown out of her matrimonial home cannot be a reason to deny interim maintenance.
An able-bodied husband cannot argue that he is not in a position to maintain his wife.
It is social, legal and morale responsibility of a man to maintain his wife and no exception to the same can be taken by us, in view of bald assertions of the appellant."

sentences.text: The finding of the court below that the revisionist was not showing emotional feeling and compassion towards her father on the dates when the case was fixed for hearing, has got no legs.
It is the duty of the father to maintain her child and the revisionist being daughter is entitled to seek maintenance from her father.
10. The court below further committed error while making observation that the mother herself was working in H.A.L., Lucknow, therefore, she has to maintain the revisionist.

The finding is further incorrect, wherein, it is observed that the mother is maintaining her daughter since 1991 and thus it is presumed that all the needs of child is being fulfilled."

Manjulata, 2001 CriLR (Raj) 57, wherein it was held that:
"16. Maintenance does not mean only a provision for food, clothing and lodging but it provides that there must be a proper provision for education of the children also.

In Nanak Chand v. Chandra Kishore Agrawal, AIR 1970 Supreme Court 446, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the Family Court must take into consideration the existing situation, including the standard of education of children, at the time of passing the order.

sentences.text: A bare perusal of the aforesaid observation clearly shows that be it under Section 24 of the HMA Act, 1955, or Section 20(3) of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, a father cannot abdicate his responsibility of looking after his unmarried daughters.
A father has a duty and an obligation to maintain his daughters and to take care of their expenses, including towards their education and marriage.
This obligation is legal and absolute in character and arises from the very existence of the relationship between the parties.
Kanya Daan is a solemn and pious obligation of a Hindu Father, from which he cannot renege.

35. Despite the applications of the Appellant being pending for claiming maintenance for the unmarried daughters, the Family Court, in the impugned order, failed to advert to any of the contentions of the Appellant.
The Family Court has not dealt with aspect of applicability of Jasbir Kaur Sehgal (supra) in the facts of the present case.

36. The Family Court, without adverting to the evidence and documents on record, in a cryptic manner, has held that Section 20 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 cannot be used to expand the provisions of Section 26, and hence major daughters of the parties are not entitled to maintenance.

This view is clearly not supported by the precedents taken note of hereinabove."
15.

Ld. Counsel has also relied upon the judgment cited as Urvashi Aggarwal v Inderpaul Aggarwal,
2021 (283) DLT 354, wherein it was held that:
"21.

sentences.text: The context of Section 125 Cr.P.C., 1973 is to ensure that the wife and the children of the husband are not left in a state of destitution after the divorce.
The husband must also carry the financial burden of making certain that his children are capable of attaining a position in society wherein they can sufficiently maintain themselves.

The mother cannot be burdened with the entire expenditure on the education of her son just because he has completed 18 years of age, and the father cannot be absolved of all responsibilities to meet the education expenses of his son because the son may have attained the age of majority, but may not be financially independent and could be incapable of sustaining himself.

A father is bound to compensate the wife who, after spending on children, may hardly be left with anything to maintain herself."
16.

sentences.text: " 11. The marriage between the parties is not in dispute.
It is settled law and even the duty of the husband to maintain his wife.
It is expected from a husband to give his wife the same standard of living which enjoys whether living jointly or separately.
In the present case, it has been shown from the record that the petitioner was having a handsome income and maintaining himself well.
There were transactions worth lakhs as per the entries of the accounts maintained by the petitioner.
It was also shown that the petitioner was having cars and several plots.

After considering all the aspects, the Trial Court rightly came to the conclusion in awarding the maintenance of Rs.35,000/- in favour of the respondent/wife being interim maintenance which is subjected to adjustment at the time of final judgment."

Counsel has further relied upon the judgment cited as Sunita Kachwaha v. Anil Kachwaha,
(2014) 16 SCC 715, wherein it was held as follows:

sentences.text: The learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the appellant-wife is well qualified, having post graduate degree in Geography and working as a teacher in Jabalpur and also working in Health Department.
Therefore, she has income of her own and needs no financial support from respondent.
In our considered view, merely because the appellant-wife is a qualified post graduate, it would not be sufficient to hold that she is in a position to maintain herself.
Insofar as her employment as a teacher in Jabalpur, nothing was placed on record before the Family Court or in the High Court to prove her employment and her earnings.
In any event, merely because the wife was earning something, it would not be a ground to reject her claim for maintenance.
The Family Court had in extenso referred to the respondent's salary and his economic condition.

The respondent is stated to be an Engineer in PHE,
Kota.
He is in Government service and according to the pay certificate then produced before the Family Court, he was getting salary of L 20,268/- per month.

In her evidence, appellant- wife has also stated that the respondent owns a very big house of his own in which he is said to have opened a hostel for boys and girls and is earning a substantial income.
She has also stated that the respondent owns another house at Talmandi Sabji Kota, Rajasthan and is receiving rental income of L 4,500/- per month.

Having regard to the salary and economic condition of the respondent, the Family Court has awarded maintenance of L 3,000/- to the wife and L 2,500/- to each of the daughters, in total L 8,000/- per month.
It is stated that the maintenance amount awarded to the daughters has been subsequently enhanced to L 10,000/- per month.
The maintenance amount of L 3,000/- per month awarded to the wife appears to be minimal and in our view, the High Court ought not to have set aside the award of maintenance.
The learned counsel for the appellants prayed for enhancement of the quantum of maintenance to the appellant-wife.

We are not inclined to go into the said submission, but liberty is reserved to the appellant- wife to seek remedy before the appropriate court."
18.

sentences.text: " 15. An order for maintenance pendente lite or for costs of the proceedings is conditional on the circumstance that the wife or husband who makes a claim for the same has no independent income sufficient for her or his support or to meet the necessary expenses of the proceeding.
It is no answer to a claim of maintenance that the wife is educated and could support herself.
Likewise, the financial position of the wife's parents is also immaterial.

The Court must take into consideration the status of the parties and the capacity of the spouse to pay maintenance and whether the applicant has any independent income sufficient for her or his support.

Maintenance is always dependent upon factual situation; the Court should, therefore, mould the claim for maintenance determining the quantum based on various factors brought before the Court."
19.

Ld. Counsel has also relied upon the judgment cited as Smt. Jasbir Kaur Sehgal v. The District Judge, Dehradun, (1997) 7 SCC 484, wherein it was held that:
"8. Wife has no fixed abode of residence.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: She says she is living in Gurdwara with her eldest daughter for safety.
On the other hand husband has sufficient income and a house to him.
Wife has not claimed any litigation expenses in this appeal.
She is aggrieved only because of the paltry amount of maintenance fixed by the courts.
No set formula can be laid for fixing the amount of maintenance.
It has, in very nature of things, to depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.
Some scope for leverage can, however, be always there.

Court has to consider the status of the parties, their respective needs, capacity of the husband to pay having regard to his reasonable expenses for his own maintenance and those he is obliged under the law and statutory but involuntary payments or deductions.

Amount of maintenance fixed for the wife should be such as she can live in reasonable comfort considering her status and the mode of life she was used to when she lived with her husband and also that she does not feel handicapped in the prosecution of her case.
At the same time, the amount so fixed cannot be excessive or extortionate.
In the circumstances of the present case we fix maintenance pendente lite at the rate of Rs. 5,000/- per month payable by respondent-husband to the appellant-wife."

20. Ld. Counsel has further relied upon the judgment cited as Naimullah Sheikh v. State of U.P.,
(Allahabad), 2024 (1) Crimes 309, wherein it was held that:
"13.

(Allahabad), 2024 (1) Crimes 309

sentences.text: In my view the legislature, while enacting this Act had this realisation in mind that though existing provision of law provide for rights of maintenance to eligible persons, however the procedural delays defeat the very purpose.
The enactment seeks to grant a quicker relief where the aggrieved woman has been subjected to domestic violence and was in a domestic relationship with the respondent.

This explains the use of words "more effective protection to women", hence it is being held that where a sufferer has a right to obtain maintenance as provided in criminal law or in civil law or personal law and that she has been subjected to domestic violence from a person who stood in domestic relationship, she may resort to quicker method of obtaining reliefs under section 12 of the Protection of Women From Domestic Violence Act,
2005.

sentences.text: From perusal of the judgments as have been referred to earlier, there remains no doubt that unmarried daughter, whether Hindu or Muslim has a right to obtain maintenance, irrespective of her age.
This is made clear again that the courts have to look for other laws applicable when the question pertains to right to be maintained.

However, where issue does not pertain to mere maintenance, the independent rights are available to an aggrieved under section 20 of the DV Act itself."
21.
Ld. Counsel for the respondent submitted that Ld. Trial Court has rightly considered all the facts and passed the order.
The complainant is much more educated.
On the other hand, the respondent is only 10th pass, he is residing in his parental home, he is unemployed and is surviving by taking loans from the relatives.
On the other hand, the appellant is working as a Teacher at Janaki Devi Public School, Jaipur, Rajasthan and is earning Rs.20,000/- per month.
Counsel submitted that she has deliberately filed the petition in Delhi though she has never resided in Delhi but she has, in order to create the jurisdiction here, shown her address in Delhi.

Ld. 
Counsel submitted that there is no income of the respondent.
On the other hand, he has a loan liability which he has borrowed and yet not paid.
He is suffering from psychiatric problem and is under treatment from MGS Medical College, MP.

She is B.Com, B.Ed. and is also taking tuitions,
even the daughter of the respondent is taking tuition and earning.
Ld. Trial Court has rightly not allowed any maintenance to the appellant and has also restricted the maintenance to the daughter on her attaining majority.
Even otherwise, there cannot be any maintenance after attaining majority under the provisions of PWDV Act.
Ld. Counsel submitted that there is no merit in the appeal, the same be dismissed.
23. After hearing the arguments and going through the record, I find that in the present case so far as the marriage is concerned, that is not disputed.
Even the fact that one girl child was born, who is presently in the care and custody of the appellant, is not disputed.
The appellant has not disputed her qualification and that she was working but has claimed that from August 2021 she is no more in job.
There are only three issues.
Firstly, the quantum of maintenance.
Secondly, the period of maintenance to the daughter and thirdly whether the appellant is also entitled to the maintenance.

24. So far as the quantum of maintenance is concerned, there are various averments made by the appellant that he is doing business under the name and style of Kalindi and is residing in his self owned accommodation.
It is also alleged that he is owning a double storey villa at Indore and a shop in MT Cloth Market in Indore.
He is B.Com and not 10th pass and doing the business of garments and bedsheets but no such document has been placed on record.
On the other hand, the respondent has also not placed any document and alleged that he is only 10th pass and is not doing anything.

The affidavits of the appellant and the respondent were also called for during the appeal and I have observed that respondent tried to conceal his income but on the other hand the appellant has also not been able to show any document with respect to the qualification and business of the respondent.
The only document, which could be placed on record, is one business card but that cannot be the basis of assessing the income.
Under the circumstances, as the Ld. Trial Court has also observed, the income of the respondent is assessed on the basis of minimum wages.

Keeping in view all these facts, in my opinion, Ld. Trial Court has rightly fixed the maintenance @ Rs.5000/- per Bindiya Kandhari @ Bindiya Arora vs Mohit Arora on 19 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/55385217/
8 month on the basis of minimum wages.

sentences.text: 25. So far as the period for which the maintenance would be payable is concerned, I find that it is the duty and responsibility of the father to maintain the unmarried daughter.

The right of the unmarried daughter to claim maintenance is recognized u/s.20(3) of Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 as also held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim 1997 (6) SCC 233, which was followed in the case of Jagdish Jugtawat v. Manjulata 2002 (5) SCC 422 and in that case the Hon'ble Apex Court applying the law laid down in Noor Saba Khatoon (Supra) held that even in the petition u/s.125 Cr.P.C. the unmarried daughter is entitled to maintenance who is dependent in order to avoid any multiplicity of litigation, it is necessary that a daughter, who is not able to maintain herself and is still studying, who is unmarried and is dependent for her survival on her parents, it is the duty and responsibility of her father to maintain her.

entities.text: Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim 1997 (6) SCC 233
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The scope under the PWDV Act is much more wider as the objective of this Act is to provide far more effective protection of the rights of women guaranteed under the circumstances, who are victims of violence of any kind occurring within the family and for matter connected therewith or incidental thereto.

Under the circumstances, the maintenance to the unmarried daughter, who is not able to maintain herself and is not earning, can be extended till she gets married or starts earning in order to firstly avoid multiplicity of litigation and secondly to also achieve the objective of PWDV Act.
Therefore, to that extent, in my opinion, order of the Ld. Trial Court is required to be changed.

The order of the trial court that maintenance would be payable till he attains majority is, therefore,
set aside.
It is ordered that respondent would continue to pay the maintenance to his daughter till she starts earning or gets married whichever is earlier.
26. So far as the maintenance to the appellant is concerned, earlier she was working.
Now she has alleged that she is no more in service from August 2021.
However, there is nothing on record to show that she is unemployed since August 2021 except her mentioning this fact in the Affidavit.
Admittedly, she was working.
It was for the appellant to show that she is no more in the employment either because she has resigned or her services have been terminated.
In the absence of any such documentary evidence being placed on the record, I find that Ld. Trial Court has rightly held that she is not entitled to any maintenance.
27. In view of the above findings, the appeal is, accordingly, disposed of.
Trial court record be sent back alongwith copy of this judgment.
Appeal file be consigned to the Record Room.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In Nanak Chand v. Chandra Kishore Agrawal, AIR 1970 Supreme Court 446, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the Family Court must take into consideration the existing situation, including the standard of education of children, at the time of passing the order.
Maintenance is always dependent upon factual situation; the Court should, therefore, mould the claim for maintenance determining the quantum based on various factors brought before the Court."

The appellant has not disputed her qualification and that she was working but has claimed that from August 2021 she is no more in job.
Secondly, the period of maintenance to the daughter and thirdly whether the appellant is also entitled to the maintenance.
The right of the unmarried daughter to claim maintenance is recognized u/s.20(3) of Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 as also held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Noor Saba Khatoon v. Mohd. Quasim 1997 (6) SCC 233, which was followed in the case of Jagdish Jugtawat v. Manjulata 2002 (5) SCC 422 and in that case the Hon'ble Apex Court applying the law laid down in Noor Saba Khatoon (Supra) held that even in the petition u/s.125 Cr.P.C. the unmarried daughter is entitled to maintenance who is dependent in order to avoid any multiplicity of litigation, it is necessary that a daughter, who is not able to maintain herself and is still studying, who is unmarried and is dependent for her survival on her parents, it is the duty and responsibility of her father to maintain her.
The scope under the PWDV Act is much more wider as the objective of this Act is to provide far more effective protection of the rights of women guaranteed under the circumstances, who are victims of violence of any kind occurring within the family and for matter connected therewith or incidental thereto.
Under the circumstances, the maintenance to the unmarried daughter, who is not able to maintain herself and is not earning, can be extended till she gets married or starts earning in order to firstly avoid multiplicity of litigation and secondly to also achieve the objective of PWDV Act.
Therefore, to that extent, in my opinion, order of the Ld. Trial Court is required to be changed.
The order of the trial court that maintenance would be payable till he attains majority is, therefore,
set aside.
However, there is nothing on record to show that she is unemployed since August 2021 except her mentioning this fact in the Affidavit.
It was for the appellant to show that she is no more in the employment either because she has resigned or her services have been terminated.
In the absence of any such documentary evidence being placed on the record, I find that Ld. Trial Court has rightly held that she is not entitled to any maintenance.
